title: ‘Aspiration clashing with reality’: Investors cool on data centres
full_text:
Data centres are becoming less appealing to big super funds and other institutions as investments due to concerns over their social licence and the time it takes to secure planning approvals.
Infrastructure Partnerships Australia chief executive Adrian Dwyer said investor appetite was cooling as operators grappled with delivering projects and meeting new guidelines from federal and state governments.
“You’re just having aspiration clash with reality,” he said.
IPA, a policy and research group representing companies and governments, and law firm Allens surveyed 26 investment institutions between late March and mid-May that collectively manage $530 billion in infrastructure assets.
Thirty-eight per cent of those surveyed singled out data centres as an asset class they would consider investing in over the next three years, compared with 70 per cent last year.
QIC Infrastructure senior principal Mitesh Kushwaha said investors were still looking at data centres but were becoming more disciplined about where they put their capital.
“Power is increasingly the gating issue. Investors need confidence that power can be delivered at scale, connections can happen on a credible time frame, and planning pathways are clear and predictable,” Kushwaha said.
Dwyer said data centres were still trying to earn their social licence amid rising community concern over where they would get power and water and how much they would use, with greater political scrutiny potentially slowing development.
Andrew Smith, co-head of Australian equities for AustralianSuper, said data centres were a critical component of the artificial intelligence expansion that would drive Australian productivity.
“The current regulatory uncertainty around investment parameters and community expectations creates a potential risk that Australia will not fully benefit from the AI buildout,” Smith said.
David Donnelly, a partner at Allens, said many big investors who had been putting money into data centres for some time were reaching their limits as they tried to maintain diversified portfolios.
“People have deployed a large amount of capital into data centres,” he said. “They just don’t have capacity to keep investing.”
New Zealand infrastructure investor Infratil, which owns almost half of Australia’s CDC Data Centres, was quizzed by investors at its annual general meeting in Wellington last month over whether it was too heavily exposed to data centres.
One investor asked whether too many were being built, creating “a lightning rod for protest, not just from whacko greenies, but from ordinary citizens who happen to be living in the vicinity of data centres”.
Infratil chief executive Jason Boyes told the meeting that CDC wanted to build data centres in industrial zones so they didn’t create “neighbour issues”. CDC accounts for about 40 per cent of Infratil’s $20.6 billion asset portfolio.
The survey found that infrastructure investors’ preferred assets are energy storage systems such as batteries, and transmission networks along with roads and water systems. Hydrogen, mining and freight rail assets are the least preferred.
This year’s survey revealed a general decline in appetite for all infrastructure assets, which Dwyer attributed to concerns over changes to capital gains tax and industrial relations as well as planning delays.
Australia, which was the most popular country to invest in last year, has dropped to second place as sentiment towards the US has rebounded. Some 80 per cent of institutions surveyed see compelling opportunities in the US, up from just 48 per cent last year.
The US was “going gangbusters” on data centres and energy generation compared with Australia’s more controlled pace, Dwyer said.
